catalog_locator: Koch 2009 p. 137, section 'System of sounds used in reconstructions' (saved ANU E Press ch. 5 PDF, page 23). Supporting primary data: Mathews & Everitt 1900 p. 265 'I. Value of letters' (archive.org scan, 'The accented syllable is marked thus ’.'; the heading 'The Gundungurra Grammar' is on the same page). Koch's word-by-word applications of the regional rule at p. 140 (Michelago), p. 148 (Jimenbuen = dyimang biwan) and pp. 158-159 (Canberra) concern Monaro and Canberra placenames that Koch assigns to Ngarigo (p. 148: 'a property near the Snowy River in the Monaro region', 'the Ngarigo language of the Monaro'; Table 5.5, p. 151: the Queanbeyan/Canberra sources 'reflect the same language as the Monaro wordlists, that is, Ngarigo'); they show how he reads the rule (per word, initial) but are not statements about nort2760.
catalog_quote: System of sounds used in reconstructions. The set of presumed consonant phonemes (distinctive sounds) for south-eastern NSW languages is given in Table 5.2, with a suggested spelling of each phoneme. ... The likely vowel phonemes are given in Table 5.4, along with English words which illustrate their normal values. ... If there was a distinctive set of long vowels these can be spelled ii, uu, and aa, with values of English beat, boot, and Bart. The stress (or emphasis) was usually on the first syllable. It is assumed that every syllable begins with a consonant sound. [Koch 2009: 137] ... Ng at the end of a syllable has the sound very nearly of ng in sing, but more nasal. The accented syllable is marked thus ’. [Mathews & Everitt 1900: 265, Gundungurra] ... The form was presumably dyimang biwan, with stress on the first syllable of each word, with the consequence that the vowel of the second syllable was spelled with an e that reflects a weaker pronunciation of /a/ in an unstressed syllable. [Koch 2009: 148, on Jimenbuen, 'a property near the Snowy River in the Monaro region', i.e. Ngarigo country, not nort2760]

The chapter is Koch's methodology chapter for the ACT and Monaro (p. 115: examples 'drawn largely from the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) and to some extent the adjacent area to the south which goes by the name Monaro'); the sound system is stated for 'south-eastern NSW languages' generally. Koch's Table 5.5 (p.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word, stated as a general property ('usually') of the south-eastern NSW languages of the ACT and adjacent region, i.e. the Ngunawal/Gundungurra area that Northern Inland Yuin covers (and Ngarigu to the south). The only primary description that marks accent, Mathews & Everitt 1900 (p. 265: 'The accented syllable is marked thus '.'), states no rule but marks the first syllable in about four-fifths of hyphenated word types (217 first vs 47 later in my tally), consistent with Koch's generalisation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing explicit. Mathews & Everitt 1900 double-mark some longer words (Gun'-dung-ur'-ra, ngun'-nun-gow'-a, yoon'-go-war'-ree, Bow'-wil-jil'-long), which suggests a second accent on a later (often third) syllable, but the source does not interpret this.
new_statements.exceptions: Koch hedges with 'usually'. Mathews & Everitt 1900 mark a non-initial accent on a minority of forms (boo-ran'-doo, thin-ba'-lee-min, ya-bil'-la, ngoo-nin'-bil, Goo-lan'-jee, bul-la-med'-dung), some of which look like compounds or pronoun-suffixed forms; no explanation offered.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Koch's phoneme/stress system is set up for reconstructing single-word placenames; Mathews & Everitt mark isolated citation forms in a paradigmatic grammar). Koch's sentence is a regional generalisation across 'south-eastern NSW languages', not a statement written for this language alone, and it rests on 1890s-1900s written records, not on speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's Northern Inland Yuin (nort2760) covers two named varieties, Gundungurra/Gandangara (ISO xrd, AIATSIS D3; Burragorang-Goulburn) and Ngunawal/Ngunnawal (ISO xul, AIATSIS S60; Yass-Canberra), which Koch treats as one language. The primary accent-marked data (Mathews & Everitt 1900) are Gundungurra from Burragorang informants Billy Russell and Bessie Sims; Mathews 1904's Ngunawal grammar has no accent marks. Koch's 2009 stress sentence is framed for 'south-eastern NSW languages' of the ACT region generally (Ngunawal-Gundungurra and Ngarigu = Southern Inland Yuin), not for nort2760 alone.

sources.note: p. 265 ('I. Value of letters'): 'The accented syllable is marked thus '.' No positional rule given, but accent is marked on every cited word. My tally of hyphenated accent-marked word types in the grammar: 217 with the mark after the first syllable (e.g. Bow'-wil 'man', Bul'-lan 'woman', jil'-long 'they', yad'-dung), 47 with a later accent (e.g. boo-ran'-doo, thin-ba'-lee-min, ya-bil'-la, ngoo-nin'-bil), 35 of the total double-marked (e.g. Gun'-dung-ur'-ra, ngun'-nun-gow'-a). Primary data only, no rule stated.
